newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-ROWELL SAFE AS ENGLAND COACH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ROWELL SAFE AS ENGLAND COACH.

text.p: Jack Rowell's position as England coach was confirmed as safe on Sunday by the powerful chairman of the Rugby Football Union's executive commitee, Cliff Brittle.

Brittle reacted swiftly to a report in the Mail On Sunday newspaper which said that after a recent meeting of the National Playing Sub Committee, Rowell was about to be axed because of the team's poor performances lately.
This season, England have beaten Italy but lost to the New Zealand Barbarians before struggling to beat Argentina 20-18.

But Brittle said in an official statement: "The RFU fully endorses the support of the current England management team and looks forward to a successful Five Nations Championship under their leadership."

The newspaper said that the National Playing Committee, which includes 1980 Grand Slam captain Bill Beaumont, Derek Morgan, who managed England's 1984 tour to South Africa, International Board representative John Jeavons-Fellows and former internationals Mark Bailey and Jeff Probyn, want Rowell to go.
The paper said they did not accept Rowell's reasons for recent poor performances and that his cavalier approach to public relations was unacceptable in the modern era.
But the RFU's statement read: "There is no truth in the story that Jack Rowell's position as England coach is under threat.

"A meeting recently took place of members of the National Playing Sub Committee to discuss a number of issues regarding the England National Team leading up to the Rugby World Cup 1999. The National Playing Sub Committee conducts regular meetings of this nature.
"The newspaper story is a misrepresentation of information appearing to eminate from a recent meeting."
Rowell has been in charge for 30 months during which England won the grand slam in 1995 and the Five Nations Championship last year. In between he took England to the semi-finals of the World Cup.

But his team's playing style and his selection policy have attracted growing criticism, though it would be unprecedented for England to switch coaches in mid-season - especially with the lack of credible alternatives.
